_meta.schema: drill: id, title, setup (how to stage it on a THROWAWAY VM), scenario (what the trainee sees), hints[] (progressive), answer {diagnosis, walkthrough}, validates (skill proven)

drills.title: The play that never starts
drills.setup: On a lab control node, add to a scratch inventory: `localhost ansible_user=nosuchuser` (no ansible_connection). Write a one-task play: create a directory, delegate_to: localhost.
drills.scenario: You run the play. The first task prints its banner and then... nothing. No error, no progress, forever.
hints: What does a hang usually mean in a batch tool?
Re-run with -vvv. Find the last line before silence.
Does it say ESTABLISH SSH CONNECTION — to localhost?

answer.diagnosis: Inventory-defined localhost without ansible_connection=local turns delegation into an SSH session to the control node, stuck at an invisible auth prompt.
answer.walkthrough: -vvv shows ESTABLISH SSH CONNECTION FOR USER nosuchuser on localhost. ansible-inventory --host localhost confirms the bad definition. Fix: add ansible_connection=local or delete the line (implicit localhost returns). Re-run: ESTABLISH LOCAL CONNECTION, task completes.

drills.title: Raw works, ping doesn't
drills.setup: On a throwaway target VM as the automation user: chmod 000 ~/.ansible (or chattr +i the tmp dir). Keep SSH keys working.
drills.scenario: ansible target -m raw -a 'id' succeeds. ansible target -m ping fails with a permission/tmpdir error.
hints: What does raw skip that ping needs?
Where does Ansible stage modules on the target?
Read the error slowly — it names a path.

answer.diagnosis: Module staging into remote_tmp (~/.ansible/tmp) is broken; transport is fine.
answer.walkthrough: raw = SSH exec only; ping = full Python module needing staging. ssh in as the automation user, try mkdir -p ~/.ansible/tmp, find the permission block, fix it (chmod 700 ~/.ansible). Re-run ping: pong. Note what pipelining WOULD have done: hidden this.

drills.title: The service that dies on arrival
drills.setup: On a lab VM: dnf install httpd; put a deliberate typo in /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf (e.g. 'Listne 80'); systemctl start httpd.
drills.scenario: systemctl start httpd returns nonzero. Your monitoring says the web tier is down.
hints: status, then journal. In that order.
journalctl -u httpd -b | tail — what's the daemon's own complaint?
Most daemons can check their own config. What's httpd's flag?

answer.diagnosis: Config syntax error; the daemon refuses to start and says so in its log.
answer.walkthrough: systemctl status httpd shows failed + exit code. journalctl -u httpd names the bad directive and line. httpd -t confirms and pinpoints. Fix the line, httpd -t clean, systemctl start, verify with ss -tlnp | grep :80 and curl localhost.

drills.validates: status→journal→validator funnel; verifying with ss/curl instead of trusting the recap

drills.title: The invisible disk eater
drills.setup: Lab VM: create a big file in /var/log, open it with `tail -f bigfile &`, then rm the file. df stays high, du can't find it.
drills.scenario: df -h says /var is 96% and climbing. du -xh /var | sort -rh finds nothing close to that size. The numbers don't add up.
hints: df counts blocks; du counts files it can NAME. What kind of file has blocks but no name?
lsof has a flag for exactly this.

answer.diagnosis: A deleted-but-open file: the name is gone, the space isn't, because a process still holds the handle.
answer.walkthrough: lsof +L1 lists processes holding deleted files — there's the tail. Kill/restart the holder (for a real service: systemctl restart). df drops instantly. Lesson: unlink removes the name; space frees when the last handle closes.

drills.title: Moved the files, broke the site
drills.setup: Lab VM with httpd working from /var/www/html. mv (not cp) an index.html in from /root. Reload the page.
drills.scenario: The page 403s. Permissions look fine — ls -l shows readable. The same file copied by hand yesterday worked.
hints: ls -l looks fine. What does ls -Z say?
mv and cp treat SELinux labels differently. Which keeps the old one?
ausearch -m AVC -ts recent — is SELinux confessing?

answer.diagnosis: mv preserved the file's admin_home_t context; httpd's domain can't read it. cp would have inherited httpd_sys_content_t from the target directory.
answer.walkthrough: ausearch shows the AVC naming httpd and the file. ls -Z confirms the wrong type. restorecon -Rv /var/www/html relabels; page loads. Permanent custom paths need semanage fcontext + restorecon.

drills.validates: mv/cp label asymmetry; AVC reading; restorecon-first instinct (never setenforce 0)

drills.title: The firewall rule that evaporated
drills.setup: Lab VM: firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp (no --permanent). Verify it's open. Then firewall-cmd --reload.
drills.scenario: The app on 8080 worked all afternoon. After a 'routine' firewall reload, clients time out. firewall-cmd --list-ports no longer shows 8080.
hints: Where do firewalld rules live — and how many places is that?

answer.diagnosis: The port was added to runtime only; --reload replaced runtime with the permanent config, which never had it.
answer.walkthrough: firewall-cmd --permanent --list-ports shows the truth (empty). Fix with the idiom: --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent && --reload. Or rescue live experiments with --runtime-to-permanent before reloads. Verify: ss -tlnp and a client connect.
